title: GRE Scores: What They Mean & How to Play the Adaptive Test
summary: The 130–170 scales, section-level adaptivity, and the pacing strategy that follows from how the GRE is built.

chunks.heading: Three scores, weighted by your field
chunks.body: You receive **Verbal 130–170**, **Quantitative 130–170** and **Analytical Writing 0–6**. There's **no single composite** — programmes read the section that matches their discipline. Percentiles tell you how you rank, which is what admissions really compare.
chunks.realExample: A 165 Quant is far more impressive percentile-wise for a humanities applicant than for an engineer, because the applicant pools differ. Judge your score against your field's typical range, not a universal bar.
chunks.memoryHook: No total score. Your field decides which of the three numbers matters.

chunks.heading: The first section decides your ceiling
chunks.body: Because Verbal and Quant are **section-level adaptive**, your **first section's performance sets the difficulty — and top possible score — of the second**. That makes the **first Verbal and first Quant sections the highest-leverage minutes on the test**.
chunks.realExample: Coasting through section 1 to 'save energy' caps your section 2 difficulty and your ceiling. Treat section 1 as the most important, not a warm-up.
chunks.memoryHook: Section 1 is the gatekeeper to the high-scoring section 2. No coasting.

chunks.heading: Use the freedom within a section
chunks.body: Within a section you can **skip, flag and revisit** questions and use a **mark-and-review** screen. So **do the easy questions first**, bank those points, and return to the hard ones — never let one stubborn question burn minutes that easy later questions need.
chunks.realExample: On a Quant section, a two-pass approach — sweep for quick wins, then circle back to the flagged hard ones — usually nets more points than grinding in order.
chunks.memoryHook: Two passes: easy wins first, hard ones flagged for later. Bank points early.

chunks.heading: Guess smart — there's no penalty
chunks.body: The GRE has **no negative marking**, so **never leave a question blank**. Before time runs out, put an answer on every question. On tough ones, **eliminate what you can** and guess from the rest to raise your odds.
chunks.realExample: 30 seconds left with three unanswered? Fill them all in — even blind guesses have a chance, and a blank is a guaranteed zero.
chunks.memoryHook: No penalty for wrong. A blank is the only guaranteed loss — always answer.

recall.q: What three scores does the GRE report, and is there a composite?
recall.a: Verbal 130–170, Quantitative 130–170 and Analytical Writing 0–6 — there is no single composite score.

recall.q: Why is the first Verbal or Quant section so important?
recall.a: The GRE is section-level adaptive, so your first section sets the difficulty and scoring ceiling of the second.

recall.q: What can you do within a GRE section that a question-adaptive test doesn't allow?
recall.a: Skip, flag and revisit questions using a mark-and-review screen.

recall.q: What's a good two-pass strategy within a section?
recall.a: Answer the easy questions first to bank points, then return to the flagged hard ones.

recall.q: Is there a penalty for wrong answers on the GRE?
recall.a: No — so never leave a question blank; always guess if needed.
